name: Tamu Lhosar
when: 15 Poush in the Nepali calendar, usually 30 December
summary: Tamu Lhosar is the Gurung new year, celebrated on 15 Poush, around 30 December, and a public holiday in Nepal. In Pokhara and Gurung villages such as Ghandruk, families gather in traditional dress for blessings, feasts, songs and dances to welcome a new animal year.
body: The Gurung, who call themselves Tamu, count years in a twelve-year cycle called Lohokor, each year represented by an animal: eagle, serpent, horse, sheep, monkey, bird, dog, deer, mouse, cow, tiger and cat. In Tamu Kyi, the Gurung language, the word is explained as Lho, new, and Sar, change, and Lhosar marks the farewell to one animal year and the welcome of the next. It falls on 15 Poush, which in most years is 30 December.

Pokhara, with its large Gurung population, is one of the best places in Nepal to see it. Community organisations hold public gatherings with stages, speeches, music and dance, and the city fills with people in Gurung dress: velvet blouses, heavy gold and coral jewellery for women, the bhangra cloth crossed over the chest for men. Lamas perform prayers, elders give blessings, and families visit one another with food and drink.

In the hill villages, Lhosar is more intimate: households clean and decorate, cook feasts of meat, sel roti and local drinks, and young people sing and dance late into the night. Many Gurung families living abroad or in Kathmandu return home for it. For visitors, Lhosar is a rare chance to see Gurung culture in its own celebration rather than a performance.
tips: Ask your hotel or guide where the main community Lhosar gatherings in Pokhara are being held that year.
Dress modestly and ask before photographing people, especially elders in traditional dress and jewellery.
Expect some offices and shops to close on the day, as Tamu Lhosar is a public holiday.
If you are trekking in late December, plan a night in a Gurung village such as Ghandruk around the date.

faqs.a: Tamu Lhosar falls on 15 Poush in the Nepali Bikram Sambat calendar, which in most years corresponds to 30 December, occasionally a day either side. It is a national public holiday in Nepal. Celebrations often begin the evening before and continue for several days in villages. Check the exact date for your year before you travel.

Tamu Lhosar is the new year of the Gurung people, who call themselves Tamu. It marks the change from one year to the next in a twelve-year cycle of animal years called Lohokor. Families gather in traditional dress for blessings by lamas and elders, feasts, songs and dances, and community events are held in Pokhara and other Gurung areas.

faqs.q: Where is the best place to see Tamu Lhosar?
faqs.a: Pokhara has large public celebrations organised by Gurung community groups, with stages, music, dance and crowds in traditional dress. For a village celebration, Gurung villages around Pokhara such as Ghandruk, Sikles or Dhampus are good, though you should go with a local guide and be invited. Kathmandu also hosts gatherings.

faqs.q: Is Tamu Lhosar the same as Tibetan Losar?
faqs.a: No. Several Himalayan peoples have their own Lhosar. Tamu Lhosar is the Gurung new year on 15 Poush, around 30 December. Sonam Lhosar of the Tamang falls in January or February, and Gyalpo Lhosar of the Sherpa and Tibetan communities in February or March. They share the idea of a new year and animal cycles but differ in dates and customs.

name: Pokhara Street Festival
when: Late December to 1 January, along Lakeside; check current dates
summary: Each year around the turn of the year, the main Lakeside road in Pokhara closes to traffic for several days of food stalls, music stages, cultural performances and crafts, ending with New Year's Eve crowds. It is the city's biggest party and a draw for Nepali visitors from across the country.
body: For a few days at the end of December, Lakeside changes character. The main road along Phewa, normally busy with taxis and scooters, is closed to vehicles and lined with stalls: grilled meat and sekuwa, momo, Newar snacks, Thakali sets, sweets and drinks, alongside handicrafts, clothing and souvenirs. Stages host bands, dance groups and cultural performances from Gurung, Magar, Tharu and other communities.

The festival is organised by local tourism bodies and businesses, and draws families from Pokhara and visitors from across Nepal and India, many timing their winter holiday around it. It builds to New Year's Eve, when the crowds are thickest and the music goes late. Hotels in Lakeside are fully booked, and prices rise.

It is not a traditional religious festival but a modern city celebration, and it makes Lakeside lively and loud. If you want quiet, stay at Damside, Fish Tail Lodge or outside the city and come in for an evening. If you enjoy crowds and street food, plan two nights in the middle of it.
tips: Book Lakeside hotels well ahead; rooms fill and prices rise for the festival and New Year.
Go in the early evening when the stalls are open but the crowds are thinner.
Keep valuables secure in the crowds, especially on New Year's Eve.
Dates and organisation change from year to year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the Pokhara Street Festival?
faqs.a: The Pokhara Street Festival is usually held over several days in late December, ending on 1 January, along the main Lakeside road. Exact dates and length are set each year by the organisers and have varied, and it has occasionally been cancelled or changed. Check current status before you travel and book accommodation early.

faqs.q: What happens at the Pokhara Street Festival?
faqs.a: The Lakeside road closes to traffic and fills with food stalls, craft and clothing stands, music stages and cultural performances by bands and dance groups. Families stroll, eat and listen to music, and crowds peak on New Year's Eve. It is a modern street celebration rather than a religious festival.

faqs.q: Is the Pokhara Street Festival crowded?
faqs.a: Yes, especially in the evenings and on New Year's Eve, when Lakeside is packed with visitors from across Nepal and India. Daytime and early evening are calmer. If you prefer quiet, stay outside central Lakeside and visit for an evening. Keep valuables secure and agree meeting points with your group.

faqs.q: Is the Pokhara Street Festival good for families?
faqs.a: In the daytime and early evening it is family-friendly, with food, music and space to walk on the closed road. Later at night, especially on New Year's Eve, crowds and noise grow, which may be too much for young children. Keep children close and agree a meeting point in case you get separated.

name: Dashain and Phulpati in Gorkha
when: Ashwin–Kartik (late September to October); Phulpati on the seventh day; dates vary each year
summary: Dashain, Nepal's longest and biggest festival, honours the goddess Durga over fifteen days. Gorkha has a special place in it: the Phulpati, a sacred bundle of leaves, flowers and plants for the goddess, is sent from Gorkha to Kathmandu, a tradition of the Shah kings, while Gorkha's Kalika temple fills with pilgrims.
body: Dashain celebrates the victory of the goddess Durga over the buffalo demon Mahishasura, and with it the victory of good over evil. It begins on Ghatasthapana, when barley seeds are sown in a sacred vessel to sprout as jamara, and builds over nine nights of worship of the goddess. On the tenth day, Vijaya Dashami, elders place red tika and jamara on the foreheads of younger family members and bless them.

The seventh day is Phulpati, meaning flowers and leaves. A bundle of sacred plants, among them banana stalk, sugarcane, pomegranate, rice and other auspicious leaves, is prepared for the goddess. By a tradition dating from the Shah kings, the Phulpati is carried from Gorkha, the dynasty's ancestral seat, to Hanuman Dhoka in Kathmandu by bearers who walk for several days, and is received there with ceremony, music and a military salute.

In Gorkha itself, Dashain brings pilgrims to the Kalika temple and Gorakhnath cave at the palace, especially on the eighth and ninth days, when animal sacrifices are made to the goddess. Bamboo swings (ping) go up in villages, children fly kites, and families gather for feasts of goat meat and sel roti. Transport is crowded as Nepalis travel home.
tips: Book buses, flights and hotels well ahead; Dashain is the busiest travel period in Nepal.
Animal sacrifices take place at temples, especially on the eighth and ninth days; decide in advance whether you want to see them.
Many offices, shops and some restaurants close around the main days; plan cash and meals accordingly.
Dates follow the lunar calendar and change every year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.a: Dashain falls in the Nepali months of Ashwin and Kartik, usually between late September and late October, following the lunar calendar. It lasts fifteen days, from Ghatasthapana to the full moon, with the main days being Phulpati (seventh), Maha Ashtami (eighth), Maha Navami (ninth) and Vijaya Dashami (tenth). Check exact dates for your year before you travel.

Phulpati, meaning flowers and leaves, is the seventh day of Dashain, when a sacred bundle of auspicious plants is brought for worship of the goddess Durga. By a tradition of the Shah kings, the Phulpati is carried from Gorkha to Hanuman Dhoka in Kathmandu over several days, and is received with ceremony and a military salute.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit Gorkha during Dashain?
faqs.a: Yes. Gorkha's palace temples are busy with pilgrims, especially on the eighth and ninth days, and the town is festive. Expect crowds, full transport and some closed shops. Animal sacrifices take place at the Kalika temple, which some visitors prefer to avoid. Dress modestly, ask before photographing worship and book hotels early.

On Vijaya Dashami, the tenth day of Dashain, elders place a tika of red vermilion mixed with rice and yoghurt on the foreheads of younger relatives, with jamara barley shoots behind the ear, and give blessings and money. Families visit relatives for several days afterwards to receive tika. Visitors may be offered tika by host families, which is an honour.
